prompt: It's snowing in Atlanta. Two inches. Describe the next six hours citywide.
response:
The first hour is still wonder. Atlanta, a city built on the assumption that ice belongs in a glass, not on a road, tilts its face up to a sky doing something it shouldn’t. Two inches of snow here isn’t weather; it’s a collective hallucination. Children who have never seen more than a dusting stand on front lawns with their tongues out, trying to catch flakes that melt before they land. The snow falls with a hushed, almost apologetic gentleness, as if it knows it’s trespassing. It blankets the dogwoods first, then the azaleas, outlining every branch in white. The light goes soft and pearlescent, and for a fleeting moment, the city is a snow globe, shaken and set down gently on a Tuesday afternoon.

By the second hour, the wonder curdles into panic. A single notification pings across a million screens: the school systems are closing early. This is the starting gun. In an instant, the collective mindset shifts from *isn’t this pretty* to *we have to get home*. The arteries begin to clog. The Perimeter, I-75, I-85, GA-400—they transform from highways into linear parking lots. A ballet of absurdity unfolds: BMWs with bald tires execute graceful, slow-motion pirouettes into curbs. Pickup trucks, driven with a confidence entirely unwarranted by two inches of powder, overtake sedans only to be found a mile ahead, hazards blinking, nosed into a ditch. The city doesn’t have enough plows, because why would it? Instead, a fleet of pickup trucks with scrap metal welded to their grilles rumbles out, privateers in a losing war. The grocery stores, already picked clean of milk and bread by a populace convinced they will be snowbound for a fortnight, are the only quiet places now.

Hour three is the hour of strandedness. The snow, no longer a novelty, is now an obstacle. It continues to fall with infuriating steadiness, packing down into a slick, gray grease on the overpasses. The interstates become a frozen river of red taillights stretching for miles. Engines are cut. People get out of their cars to stretch, to commiserate, to look at the sky with a growing sense of dread. The city’s famous canopy of trees, still holding onto their leaves, begins to betray us. The wet, heavy snow loads every limb. You can hear it—a percussive, unsettling soundtrack of cracks and groans, followed by the thud of a limb shearing off, sometimes taking a power line with it. Across the metro area, pockets of darkness begin to bloom. Inside those dark houses, the gas fireplaces and camping stoves are lit, and the first board games are brought down from dusty shelves.

Hour four. The gridlock is now absolute. The mayor is on every channel, asking people who are already iced in place to please stay off the roads. The salt trucks, few and far between, are themselves stuck in the traffic. The city is a living diorama of poor planning and Southern stubbornness. On the side streets, a new culture emerges. Teenagers on dirt bikes and four-wheelers, machines usually confined to muddy pastures, become the only functioning transport. They tow sleds behind them, delivering groceries, giving rides, becoming improbable heroes. The social contract rewrites itself in real time: strangers push a stranded nurse’s car up a hill, a corner bodega stays open late to serve hot coffee to the walking refugees, a man with a winch on his Jeep pulls a MARTA bus from a snowy embankment.

By the fifth hour, a profound and exhausted silence descends. The snow has stopped, and the temperature is plummeting, glazing the two inches of powder with a hard, crystalline crust. The city is no longer a snow globe; it’s a landscape trapped under glass. The abandoned cars, hundreds of them, sit at surreal angles on the interstates, their windshields a gallery of crude finger-drawn messages: *BE BACK*, *HELP*, *OUT OF GAS*. The soundscape has shifted. The constant hum of Atlanta—the drone of tires on pavement—is gone, replaced by the sharp crack of freezing tree limbs and the distant, futile whine of spinning tires. The air is clean and knifelike. The sky clears, and a hard, cold moon illuminates a Southern city that has been humbled, transformed into a strange, silent, and glittering sculpture of its former self.

Hour six. The deep freeze begins. The two inches of snow, so charming this morning, is now a single, city-wide sheet of black ice, invisible and lethal. The city isn’t sleeping; it’s hibernating in a state of emergency. In living rooms from Buckhead to Bankhead, the same scene plays out: families gathered under blankets, power out, eating cold fried chicken by candlelight, the kids finally asleep after the sugar rush of a snow day that turned apocalyptic. The highways are silent, silver ribbons. The only movement is the slow, orange blink of emergency vehicles creeping along the shoulders, checking on the stranded. Atlanta, for the first time in decades, is completely still. The two inches of snow have done what nothing else could: they stopped the capital of the New South dead in its tracks, a beautiful, fragile, and utterly paralyzed kingdom of ice.
